claim: Axons span extreme distances and are subject to significant stretch deformations during limb movements or sudden head movements, especially during impacts.
source: Axons span extreme distances and are subject to significant stretch deformations during limb movements or sudden head movements, especially during impacts.
evidence: This is a general statement about axonal properties presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Chick dorsal root ganglion axons exhibit a tension buffering or strain-softening response, where its steady state elastic modulus decreases with increasing strain.
source: Using a custom developed force apparatus, we demonstrate that chick dorsal root ganglion axons exhibit a tension buffering or strain-softening response, where its steady state elastic modulus decreases with increasing strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the custom force apparatus described in the manuscript.

claim: The recently discovered membrane-associated actin-spectrin scaffold plays a prominent mechanical role in axons.
source: We then explore the contributions from the various cytoskeletal components of the axon to show that the recently discovered membrane-associated actin-spectrin scaffold plays a prominent mechanical role.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cytoskeletal perturbation experiments and knockdown studies.

claim: The actin-spectrin skeleton acts as an axonal tension buffer by reversibly unfolding repeat domains of the spectrin tetramers to release excess mechanical stress.
source: Finally, using a theoretical model, we argue that the actin-spectrin skeleton acts as an axonal tension buffer by reversibly unfolding repeat domains of the spectrin tetramers to release excess mechanical stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical modeling combined with experimental observations.

claim: Microtubules and their associated proteins are not the only significant load-bearing elements in axons.
source: Our results revise the current viewpoint that microtubules and their associated proteins are the only significant load-bearing elements in axons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the significant contribution of F-actin and spectrin to axonal mechanics.

claim: Axons have an axi-symmetric structure with a central core of aligned microtubules arranged in a polar fashion and cross-linked by associated proteins.
source: It has an axi-symmetric structure with a central core of aligned microtubules arranged in a polar fashion and cross-linked by associated proteins (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of axonal ultrastructure supported by reference to Figure 1 and established knowledge.

claim: The axonal core is surrounded by neurofilaments and a membrane-associated cortex of cross-linked actin filaments.
source: This core is surrounded by neurofilaments and a membrane-associated cortex of cross-linked actin filaments (Alberts et al., 2002).
evidence: This structural description is supported by citation to Alberts et al., 2002.

claim: The actin cortex involves a periodic array of F-actin rings which are interconnected by spectrin cross-bridges.
source: Recent experiments using super-resolution light microscopy have revealed that the actin cortex also involves a periodic array of F-actin rings which are interconnected by spectrin cross-bridges (Xu et al., 2013; D'Este et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to super-resolution microscopy studies.

claim: Mammalian sciatic nerves can experience localized strains up to 30% during regular limb movements.
source: Mammalian sciatic nerves, for example, can experience localized strains up to 30% during regular limb movements (Phillips et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Phillips et al., 2004.

claim: Nerves running along the mouth-floor of certain species of baleen whales can experience stretching up to 160% during feeding.
source: A much more extreme case of stretching occurs in the nerves running along the mouth-floor of certain species of baleen whales where it can reach up to 160% during feeding, and these axons have evolved special strategies to cope with such situations (Lillie et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lillie et al., 2017.

claim: Recent in vivo studies in humans have shown significant changes in nerve stiffness due to limb flexion.
source: Recent in vivo studies in humans have shown significant changes in nerve stiffness due to limb flexion (Andrade et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Andrade et al., 2016.

claim: The brain undergoes significant shear deformations (2–5% strain) even under normal activities such as jumping.
source: It is also known that the brain, being one of the softest tissues, undergoes significant shear deformations (2–5% strain) even under normal activities such as jumping (Bayly et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bayly et al., 2005.

claim: There are an estimated 1.6 to 3.6 million cases of traumatic brain concussions annually in the USA.
source: At higher accelerations, transient to traumatic brain concussions occur and is a leading cause of injury in contact sports, with an estimated 1.6 to 3.6 million cases annually in the USA alone (Harmon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harmon et al., 2013.

claim: Axons respond viscoelastically to stretch deformations.
source: Pioneering experiments by Heidemann and co-workers show that axons respond viscoelastically to stretch deformations (Dennerll et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dennerll et al., 1989.

claim: Axons can develop excess tension when stretched, presumably due to the action of molecular motors.
source: Besides, they have shown that axons can also develop excess tension when stretched, presumably due to the action of molecular motors (Dennerll et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dennerll et al., 1989.

claim: Contractile stress generation in axons arises due to the action of myosin-II molecular motors.
source: Such contractile stress generation has since been studied experimentally and theoretically in some detail and is found to arise due to the action of myosin-II molecular motors (Bernal et al., 2007; O'Toole et al., 2015; Tofangchi et al., 2016; Mutalik et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental and theoretical studies.

claim: The force relaxation after each strain step is indicative of the viscoelastic nature of the axon.
source: The force relaxation after each step is indicative of the viscoelastic nature of the axon.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Axonal tension tends to relax to the same steady state value as the strain on the axon increases (tension homeostasis).
source: The calculated tension plotted in Figure 2B shows that it tends to relax to the same steady state value 𝒯ss as the strain on the axon increases (tension homeostasis).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The occurrence of a steady state tension after each strain step is indicative of a solid-like behavior of the axons at longer timescales.
source: The occurrence of a steady state tension (or a steady state force) after each strain step is indicative of a solid-like behavior of the axons at longer timescales when probed at room temperature to suppress growth and other active responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The force decays to a non-zero steady state value after a strain step with wait time ∼10 min.
source: To check this further, we performed a few experiments with wait time ∼10 min >> the typical relaxation time (quantified later) after a strain step and these show that the force indeed decays to a non-zero steady state value (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chick DRG axons are about 1 µm thick and the actin-spectrin rings in them are about 200 nm apart.
source: The chick DRG axons we use are about 1 µm thick and the rings in them are about 200 nm apart (corresponds to the length of a single tetramer as shown in Refs [Xu et al., 2013; D'Este et al., 2015]).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements and citations to previous studies.

claim: The elastic modulus of axons shows strain-softening which reflects the tendency for tension to saturate with increasing strain.
source: Remarkably, the elastic modulus showsstrain-softening which reflect the tendency for tension to saturate with increasing strain (tension homeostasis).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The strain-softening response is not due to any permanent damage or plastic flow as the response remains qualitatively the same when repeated for the same axon.
source: This strain-softening response is not due to any permanent damage or plastic flow as the response remains qualitatively the same when repeated for the same axon.
evidence: This claim is based on repeated measurements on the same axons.

claim: When axons are released from the cantilever from the maximal strain state they recover their initial length within 5–10 s.
source: Moreover, when the axons are released from the cantilever from the maximal strain state they recover their initial length within 5–10 s (Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by video data (Figure 2—video 2).

claim: Taxol treatment at 10 µM for 30 min results in axons showing strain-softening response with higher values of the moduli compared to normal axons.
source: We first tested the response of axons treated with the microtubule stabilizer Taxol at 10 µM for 30 min and the resulting data are shown in Figure 3A. The elastic moduli show a strain-softening response similar to normal axons, albeit with higher values of the moduli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: F-actin-stabilized axons (treated with 5 µM Jasplakinolide for 30 min) exhibit a more substantial increase in the elastic moduli compared to Taxol treatment, while both display pronounced strain-softening.
source: Next, in order to check whether F-actin dynamics could lead to strain-softening, we treated neurons with 5 µM of the F-actin stabilizing agent Jasplakinolide for 30 min; see Figure 3B. As shown in Figure 3C, F-actin-stabilized axons exhibit a more substantial increase in the elastic moduli compared to Taxol treatment, while both display pronounced strain-softening.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: No distinction could be seen between Blebbistatin-treated (30 µM for 30 min) and untreated cells in terms of axonal response.
source: Next, even though our experiments were performed at room temperature to suppress motor activity (Yengo et al., 2012; Hong et al., 2016), in order to check whether the axonal response is influenced by acto-myosin contractility as reported in Tofangchi et al. (2016); Mutalik et al. (2018), we incubated the cells with 30 µM Blebbistatin for 30 min and checked their response as above (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). No distinction could be seen between treated and untreated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2, and citations.

claim: Treatment with Nocodazole (10 µM) for up to 30 min results in a reduction in steady state tension in axons.
source: We then performed measurements after depolymerizing microtubules using Nocodazole (Noco) at 10 µM for up to 30 min. After this treatment, some axons exhibited pronounced beading (Pearling Instability) as is expected when microtubules are lost (Datar et al., 2019). As can be seen from Figure 3D, on the average, treated axons showed a reduction in steady state tension: 𝒯ss(γ=0.01)=9.3 nN±1.6(control) , 6.4 nN±2.1(Noco: 5 min), 5.8 nN±2.0( Noco: 30 min) where the values are mean ± SE (see Figure 3E, and individual data in Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E, and citation to Datar et al., 2019.

claim: Treatment with Latrunculin-A (1 µM) for up to 30 min produces a much more dramatic reduction in the steady state tension than Nocodazole.
source: Next, we disrupted F-actin using 1 µM Latrunculin-A (Lat-A) for up to 30 min and observed that this treatment produced a much more dramatic reduction in the steady state tension than did Nocodazole, as shown in Figure 3D. In this case, we obtained, 𝒯ss(γ=0.01)=13.0 nN±2.5(control ), 3.5 nN±1.0(Lat-A: 5 min), 1.8 nN±0.4(Lat-A: 30 min), where the values are mean ± SE (see Figure 3F, and individual data in Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3F.

claim: The tension relaxation is much faster for Latrunculin-A treatment as compared with either Nocodazole-treated or control axons.
source: In addition, the tension relaxation is much faster for Latrunculin-A treatment as compared with either Nocodazole-treated or control axons (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 5), suggesting that F-actin plays a leading role in axonal mechanics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: Actin disruption leading to axon softening is not accompanied by microtubule disassembly.
source: Comparing these results with those without Taxol treatment suggests that actin disruption leading to axon softening is not accompanied by microtubule disassembly.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing experimental results with and without Taxol pre-treatment.

claim: Every axon imaged (n = 180) showed significant spectrin fluorescence distributed all along the axon even at 2-DIV.
source: To check the spectrin distribution along axons we first imaged spectrin content in chick DRG axons using antibody labelling and confocal microscopy. Every axon imaged (n = 180) showed significant spectrin fluorescence distributed all along the axon even at 2-DIV (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The periodic actin-spectrin lattice becomes more prevalent with the number of days the neurons are in culture while maintaining a periodicity in the range of 190 to 200 nm.
source: The periodic lattice becomes more prevalent with the number of days the neurons are in culture while maintaining a periodicity in the range of 190 to 200 nm (Appendix 1—table 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 for quantification).
evidence: This claim is supported by STED microscopy data quantified in Appendix 1—table 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The periodic actin-spectrin skeleton is well preserved after treatment with either Taxol or Jasplakinolide for 30 min.
source: To check the effect of the different drug treatments on the periodic lattice, we did super-resolution imaging of 2-DIV cells after treating them with the stabilizing drugs Taxol or Jasplakinolide for 30 min. The periodic skeleton is well preserved after treatment with either of these drugs. In vehicle control, 32 out of 36 axons showed rings; after treatment with Jasplakinolide, 28 out of 31 showed rings; and after exposure to Taxol, 31 out of 32 showed rings.
evidence: This claim is supported by super-resolution imaging data.

claim: After treatment with Nocodazole, 15 out of 23 axons showed rings.
source: After treatment with Nocodazole, 15 out of 23 axons showed rings.
evidence: This claim is supported by super-resolution imaging data.

claim: After treatment with Latrunculin-A, no clear signature of periodic rings could be seen in 17 out of 19 axons, and the periodicity is lost.
source: We also did treatment with Latrunculin-A and no clear signature of periodic rings could be seen in 17 out of 19 axons. Most notably, the periodicity is lost after Lat-A treatment (see Figure 4A3; and also Figure 4—figure supplement 4 for quantification).
evidence: This claim is supported by super-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 4A3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The increase in the prevalence of the actin-spectrin lattice with age correlates well with the mechanical response, with axons of older neurons showing much higher values of Young's moduli for all strain values.
source: Remarkably, the increase in the prevalence of the actin-spectrin lattice with age quantified in Appendix 1—table 1 correlates well with the mechanical response, with axons of older neurons showing much higher values of Young's moduli for all strain values as can be seen from Figure 4B.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation between STED microscopy data (Appendix 1—table 1) and mechanical measurements (Figure 4B).

claim: Anti-β-II spectrin morpholino-treated axons show a dramatic decrease in the steady state tension compared to axons treated with a non-specific morpholino.
source: Next, we performed knock-down experiments using a specific morpholino (MO) against chick β-II spectrin. Depletion of β-II spectrin has been reported to abolish the development of the periodic organization of the actin-spectrin membrane-associated skeleton (Zhong et al., 2014). Anti-β-II spectrin morpholino-treated axons show a dramatic decrease in the steady state tension compared to axons treated with a non-specific morpholino as shown in Figure 4C.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and citation to Zhong et al., 2014.

claim: The extent of spectrin knock-down was quantified using antibody labeling and demonstrates a correlation between reduction in spectrin content and strain-dependent steady state tension.
source: The extent of knock-down was quantified using antibody labeling and the result is shown in the inset of Figure 4C, demonstrating a correlation between reduction in spectrin content and strain-dependent steady state tension shown in the main plot.
evidence: This claim is supported by antibody labeling data shown in the inset of Figure 4C.

claim: AFM experiments show that spectrin repeats sequentially unfold under tension.
source: Moreover, AFM experiments show that spectrin repeats sequentially unfold under tension (Rief et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rief et al., 1999.

claim: Tau proteins, which crosslink microtubules in axons, unfold under tension.
source: Tau proteins, which crosslink microtubules in axons, unfold under tension (Wegmann et al., 2011), resulting in viscoelastic solid-like behavior (Ahmadzadeh et al., 2014; Ahmadzadeh et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wegmann et al., 2011, Ahmadzadeh et al., 2014, and Ahmadzadeh et al., 2015.

claim: The model predicts a non-monotonic dependence of the tension relaxation time τ on strain.
source: With our model, we also predict a surprising, non-monotonic dependence of the tension relaxation time τ on strain; see Figure 5C.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The maximum number of spectrin molecules in a cylindrical cross-section of a typical axon can be estimated to be about 300, or more conservatively about 180.
source: An order of magnitude estimate of the maximum possible contribution coming from spectrin tetramers to axonal tension can be made as follows. If we assume the width of a spectrin molecule to be 10 nm, and take a typical axon diameter as 1 µm, the maximum number of spectrin molecules (for a mature axon, say) in a cylindrical cross-section can be estimated to be about 300. A more conservative estimate can be made using available data from RBCs (Liu et al., 1987), where the actin-spectrin junction is reported to be 35 nm in width (with each junction connecting to an alpha and a beta spectrin molecule), and thus a number closer to 180.
evidence: This is an estimate based on geometric calculations and citation to Liu et al., 1987.

claim: The spectrin contribution to axonal tension can be estimated to be of the order of 𝒯ss∼6-10 nN.
source: AFM pulling experiments on native spectrin showed that the force-extension curve first rapidly increased (due to entropic stiffening), and then, due to repeat unfolding, underwent a succession of sharp peaks and drops, bound below by a gently increasing, plateau-like force of about 30 pN (Rief et al., 1999). From this, we can estimate the spectrin contribution to axonal tension to be of the order of 𝒯ss∼6-10 nN.
evidence: This is an estimate based on AFM data from Rief et al., 1999 and the number of spectrin molecules calculated.

claim: The estimated spectrin contribution to axonal tension (6-10 nN) is comparable to the axon tension for 4-DIV axons.
source: These values are comparable to the axon tension for 4-DIV axons (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a comparison between the estimated spectrin contribution and measured axon tension data.

claim: In C. elegans, the axons of spectrin knock-out animals are known to snap during normal wiggling of the worm.
source: Notably, in C. elegans, the axons of spectrin knock-out animals are known to snap during normal wiggling of the worm, although the exact nature of axonal deformation (buckling vs stretch) that causes damage is unclear (Hammarlund et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hammarlund et al., 2007.

claim: The use of a FRET-based spectrin tension sensor has shown that β-spectrin in C. elegans axons are held under pre-stress.
source: Moreover, the use of a FRET-based spectrin tension sensor has shown that β-spectrin in C. elegans axons are held under pre-stress; and this is further supported by axonal retraction observed after laser ablation (Krieg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krieg et al., 2014.

claim: Spectrin-mediated elastic behavior leading to strain softening has been documented in experimental and theoretical studies on Red Blood Cells (RBCs).
source: In contrast, spectrin-mediated elastic behavior leading to strain softening has been documented in experimental and theoretical studies on Red Blood Cells (RBCs), which have a membrane-associated hexagonal actin-spectrin skeleton (Lee and Discher, 2001; Gov, 2007; Zhu and Asaro, 2008; Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to RBC studies.

claim: The current view is that RBC softening is most likely due to the unfolding of spectrin domains under force.
source: The current view is that RBC softening is most likely due to the unfolding of spectrin domains under force (Johnson et al., 2007; Krieger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2007 and Krieger et al., 2011.

claim: The axonal response reported here is in sharp contrast with the strain stiffening response exhibited by many cell types.
source: The axonal response reported here is in sharp contrast with the strain stiffening response exhibited by many cell types (Fernández et al., 2006; Kollmannsberger and Fabry, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison between the axonal response and other cell types, supported by citations.

claim: Strain stiffening in many cell types has its origin in the entropic nature of the F-actin cytoskeleton and has been observed in purified systems of a variety of biopolymers.
source: This stiffening has its origin in the entropic nature of the F-actin cytoskeleton and has been observed in purified systems of a variety of biopolymers (Storm et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Storm et al., 2005.

claim: The stiffening response can transition toward a softening response at higher strains, either due to the force-induced detachment of transient cross-links or due to buckling of filaments.
source: It is also known that the stiffening response can transition toward a softening response at higher strains, either due to the force-induced detachment of transient cross-links or due to buckling of filaments (Gardel et al., 2004; Chaudhuri et al., 2007; Åström et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gardel et al., 2004, Chaudhuri et al., 2007, and Åström et al., 2008.

claim: Eukaryotic cells show a transient softening following a fast stretch and release protocol, which is a transient effect not reflected in the steady state modulus.
source: It has been reported that eukaryotic cells show a transient softening following a fast stretch and release protocol (Trepat et al., 2007). This is a transient effect and is not reflected in the steady state modulus of the cell and has been attributed to ATP driven processes, which make the cell behave as a soft-glassy system (Trepat et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Trepat et al., 2007 and Trepat et al., 2008.

claim: Spectrin mutations are associated with neurological disorders like spinocerebellar ataxia.
source: From a medical point of view, spectrin mutations are associated with neurological disorders like spinocerebellar ataxia (Ikeda et al., 2006) and early infantile epileptic encephalopathies (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ikeda et al., 2006 and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Spectrin mutations are associated with early infantile epileptic encephalopathies.
source: From a medical point of view, spectrin mutations are associated with neurological disorders like spinocerebellar ataxia (Ikeda et al., 2006) and early infantile epileptic encephalopathies (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Fertilised Giriraja-2 chicken eggs were obtained from Karnataka Veterinary, Animal and Fisheries Sciences University, Bangalore, India.
source: Fertilised Giriraja-2 chicken eggs were obtained from Karnataka Veterinary, Animal and Fisheries Sciences University, Bangalore, India.
evidence: This is a statement about the source of materials used in the study.

claim: The eggs were incubated for 8–9 days and Dorsal Root Ganglia (DRG) were isolated and dissociated using a standard protocol.
source: The eggs were incubated for 8–9 days and Dorsal Root Ganglia (DRG) were isolated and dissociated using a standard protocol.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: All neurons transfected with carboxyfluorescein tagged control MO (n = 46) showed diffuse fluorescence in the soma and all along the axon indicating the presence of tagged MO in the cytosol.
source: The transfection conditions were optimized by fluorescence microscopy using a carboxyorescein tagged control MO (5'-CCTCTTACCTCAGTTACAATTTATA-3'). All neurons (n = 46) showed diffuse fluorescence in the soma and all along the axon indicating the presence of tagged MO in the cytosol.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The periodicity of the actin-spectrin lattice corresponds to the α/β spectrin tetramer length which is about 190 nm.
source: The inset shows sample intensity-intensity autocorrelation functions for different DIV axons. The periodicity corresponds to the α/β spectrin tetramer length which is about 190 nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by autocorrelation analysis shown in the inset of Figure 4B.

claim: The setup was tested using another cantilever as mock sample and this gave the expected linear elastic response.
source: The setup was tested using another cantilever as mock sample and this gave the expected linear elastic response.
evidence: This describes a control experiment to validate the force measurement apparatus.

claim: All experiments were performed at room temperature (25–26 °C) to suppress active dynamics as much as possible.
source: In order to suppress active dynamics as much as possible, we performed all experiments at room temperature (25–26 °C) (Yengo et al., 2012; Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions, supported by citations.
